item.title: Learning to Flexibly Respond to Performance Difficulties
item.description:
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

Learning to Flexibly Respond to Performance Difficulties

Relieving the emotional burden of problems and fixing them with a share.

Posted September 13, 2026

Key points
  • Problem sharing with teammates, coaches, and others can relieve emotional burden.
  • Owning problems by sharing them can open the door to responding effectively to them.
  • Psychological flexibility allows the ability to make adjustments and effectivelly perform despite problems.
Sharing challenges with teammates and coaches can deliver valued results.
Source: Photo courtesy of LuigiNovi/Wikimedia Commons

“A problem shared is a problem halved.”

That’s a proverb, introduced in a November 1931 edition of English newspaper The Morecambe Guardian. It derived from “trouble shared is trouble halved,” a quote from fictitious character, Lord Peter Wimsey, in the book Five Red Herrings (1931), scribed by author Dorothy L. Sayers.

Abiding that proverb will assist in improving athletic performance and life experiences.

Sharing a problem eases emotional burden because it’s a step towards accepting it rather than denying it or trying to erase it from memory. Attempting to ignore a problem only makes it worse because it results in mental dwelling on it, instead of effectively responding to the problem. Unfortunately, there’s no delete button installed in your head.

According to Acceptance and Commitment Training (ACT), a popular approach to clinical and sports psychology, acceptance means acknowledging the problem and its accompanying thoughts and feelings, plus a willingness to experience that inside stuff, instead of trying to eliminate it.

By sharing troubling circumstances, and the unwanted thoughts and emotions that tag along with them, they are accepted and allowed for, enabling the ability to respond effectively with what ACT calls committed actions. Doing so assists in thriving rather than suffering.

Sports participation, and the rest of life, can deliver bothersome, punch-in-the-face circumstances. It's how we respond to them that makes the difference in a good or bad way. Acceptance, assisted by sharing, opens the door for identifying and choosing effective responses to problematic experiences.

Disclosing a problem not only eases emotional burden, it also enables ownership of the trouble. Ownership doesn’t signify self-blame for whatever happens. It does mean that we must recognize that it is our responsibility to effectively respond to it.

Taking such ownership requires awareness, another cornerstone of ACT. Awareness consists of in-the-moment presence to clearly observe the context (surrounding circumstances), including thoughts, emotions, and bodily feelings, that allows for effective orientation and behavioral decision making.

Taking Ownership to Move Forward

Problems in sports are a normal experience and can be distressing as number 23's body language communicates, here. Sharing can relieve and lead to learning something to remedy the problem.
Source: Photo by Tomas Kovala, courtesy of Wikimedia Commons

Problems--errors in play and interpersonal difficulties-- are a normal and unavoidable aspect of the sports experience.

Making a mistake during performance can be painful. Many athletes will deny responsibility for their error, blaming a teammate or a referee, which gives short-term relief from their embarrassment, frustration, etc. It can also alienate you from the team, and result in the failure to own the miscue and learn from it.

Owning the performance mistake by sharing it with the instructor or coach will keep it from escalating into an emotional mental distraction. It also allows the ability to learn from it and minimize the chances of the miscue repeating itself.

Awareness of the hurt and distraction we inflict on a teammate by publicly chastising and humiliating them for a mistake they made, and accompanying guilt we experience for our disrespectful behavior, enables the sharing of guilt and an apology to the person we injured.

Such ownership not only eases the burden of guilt, but it also enables ownership of the mistake, opening the door for demonstrating responsibility and making behavioral adjustments to prevent future disrespectful outbursts.

Losing an important game due to a mistake you made could be etched in your memory forever. Sharing that mistake and the mental anguish tagging along with it not only provides immediate relief, but it can also enable lifelong acceptance of what happened, so whenever the memory shows up, you won’t suffer or be distracted by it. Repeated sharing further strengthens that acceptance.

article continues after advertisement

Share It, Own It, and Flexibly Perform

Such mental maneuvering, described above, is what ACT calls psychological flexibility, defined by Acceptance and Commitment Training creator Steven C. Hayes as “the ability to contact the present moment fully and without needless defense, and to persist in the service of chosen values.”

Owning a problem by openly sharing it with a coach, teammate, or parent enables psychological flexibility, including relief of mental burden and adjustments for improved play and performance

A problem shared is a problem halved!
